title: Model
text:
Code
import os

import duckdb
import pandas as pd
from pins import board_folder
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from vetiver import VetiverModel, vetiver_pin_write

title: Model
text:
Get Data
Load the Palmer Penguins data and retain observations with complete values for the model outcome and predictors.


Code
con = duckdb.connect("my-db.duckdb")
df = con.execute("SELECT * FROM penguins").fetchdf()
con.close()

model_columns = [
    "bill_length_mm",
    "species",
    "sex",
    "body_mass_g",
]

model_df = df.dropna(subset=model_columns)
retained_n = len(model_df)
excluded_n = len(df) - len(model_df)


The model retains 333 of 344 observations and excludes 11 observations with missing values in the model outcome or predictors.

title: Model
text:
Define Model and Fit
Fit a linear regression predicting body mass from bill length, species, and sex. Convert categorical predictors into indicator variables.


Code
X = pd.get_dummies(model_df[["bill_length_mm", "species", "sex"]], drop_first=True)
y = model_df["body_mass_g"]

model = LinearRegression().fit(X, y)

title: Model
text:
Evaluate Model
Perform basic checks that the model ran successfully.


Code
print(f"Training R^2 {model.score(X, y)}")
print(f"Intercept {model.intercept_}")
print(f"Columns {X.columns}")
print(f"Coefficients {model.coef_}")

title: Model
text:
Create a Vetiver Model
Vetiver is Posit’s opinionated framework for packaging and publishing models, creating prediction APIs, and monitoring model performance. The VetiverModel class wraps a model and its metadata, including a description and prototype data.


Code
v = VetiverModel(model, model_name="penguin_model", prototype_data=X)
print(v.description)
print(v.prototype)


A scikit-learn LinearRegression model
<class 'vetiver.types.prototype'>

title: Model
text:
Store and Version the Model
Store and version the model on a pins board. The board can use a local folder, Posit Connect, Amazon S3, and more. Writing the vetiver model to the board stores the binary model object and metadata like packages needed for prediction and the model’s input data prototype for checking new data.


Code
model_folder = os.getenv(
    "PENGUIN_MODEL_BOARD",
    "C:/Users/mpfol/OneDrive/Documents/penguin-artifacts/model",
)
model_board = board_folder(model_folder, allow_pickle_read=True)
vetiver_pin_write(model_board, v)


Model Cards provide a framework for transparent, responsible reporting. 
 Use the vetiver `.qmd` Quarto template as a place to start, 
 with vetiver.model_card()
Writing pin:
Name: 'penguin_model'
Version: 20261127T123902Z-42702

title: Model
section: Check: Load Saved Model and Predict
text:
Check: Load Saved Model and Predict
Test that the model can be loaded from the board in a new session. The model object and metadata are restored.


Code
loaded_v = VetiverModel.from_pin(model_board, "penguin_model")
print(loaded_v.description)

new_penguin = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "bill_length_mm": [39.1],
        "species_Chinstrap": [False],
        "species_Gentoo": [False],
        "sex_male": [True],
    }
)

loaded_v.model.predict(new_penguin)

title: Penguin Explorer
text:
Explore the relationship between penguin bill length and body mass using the Palmer Penguins dataset.
This is a learning project following Alex K. Gold’s DevOps for Data Science.

title: Penguin Explorer
text:
Current progress
The local labs for Chapters 1 through 4 are complete:

R and Python use project-specific environments with recorded dependencies.
The EDA and model reports read a shared DuckDB database.
A saved model is served through a local Vetiver prediction API.
A Shiny interface requests predictions and logs successes, diagnostic details, and request failures.

Use the navigation to explore the R EDA and Python model reports. The interactive prediction interface requires the separate Shiny and API servers to be running; startup commands and project progress are documented in the repository README.
Rebuilding and publishing this Quarto website through GitHub Actions is the next chapter’s task.

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
The dataset contains 344 penguins from three species observed between 2007 and 2009. Most measurement variables have two missing values, while sex has 11; this missingness should be considered before modeling or comparing groups.


Code
df |>
  dplyr::summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.)))) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "missing_values"
  )


# A tibble: 8 × 2
  variable          missing_values
  <chr>                      <int>
1 species                        0
2 island                         0
3 bill_length_mm                 2
4 bill_depth_mm                  2
5 flipper_length_mm              2
6 body_mass_g                    2
7 sex                           11
8 year                           0


The plot excludes 2 penguins with missing values for bill length, or body mass.


Code
plot_df |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, color = species)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point() +
  ggplot2::geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, formula = "y ~ x") +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = "Penguin Bill Length vs Body Mass",
    x = "Bill Length (mm)",
    y = "Body Mass (g)",
    color = "Species"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal()









Across all penguins, longer bills are generally associated with greater body mass, but the species form distinct clusters. All three species show positive fitted slopes, with Gentoo’s steepest; the overall pattern partly reflects both within-species association and differences among species.
